releases.body:
### Added

* `python -m perun mcp-health [--all] [--fix] [--selftest] [--json]` diagnoses
  the Perun MCP connection: the state OpenCode holds for the directory, the
  measured cost of the last start, and the remedy. `--fix` disconnects and
  reconnects the server — the only way out of a connection wedged in `pending`,
  where a plain connect keeps answering the half-open attempt — and `--all`
  does it for every location the service knows plus every registered project,
  because the client keeps one connection **per directory** and caches a failure
  for all sessions in it. `--selftest` performs the client's own stdio handshake,
  timed, so a healthy server can be proven before the editor is blamed. Exit
  code 0 means every location was **verified**: the service answered and the
  server is connected there (or is genuinely not configured). A service that
  cannot be asked is reported as unreachable and fails the command, because
  "could not ask" must never read as "nothing to fix".
* Every MCP start records its measured cost in `PERUN_HOME/mcp-startup.json`, so
  a start creeping towards the client's 60 s deadline is visible instead of
  guessed at. The record describes exactly one run — the newest start — and each
  write carries its own `pid`, so concurrent starts (one server per location)
  replace each other instead of merging into a record that is true of neither.

### Fixed

* `perun mcp-health` no longer reports an unreachable OpenCode service as "not
  configured" with exit code 0 (and the advice to add an MCP entry that is
  already there). `server_status()` now says whether the connection state could
  be read at all, the verdict is `service_unreachable` with the remedy to start
  or repair the service, and such a location fails the run. `--all` with no
  location to check also exits non-zero instead of succeeding on an empty check.
* An OpenCode service that *answered* with an error status is no longer called
  unreachable: the verdict is `service_error` and the remedy points at the
  service log (and the HTTP status) instead of telling the operator to start a
  service that is already running.
* A location that reports no `perun` server is now given time to appear before it
  is judged. Reading `/api/mcp` is what makes OpenCode materialize a location,
  and the connect is asynchronous — measured as no row at t+0, `pending` at
  t+2 s, `connected` at t+4 s — so the previous single re-read landed in that gap
  and reported "not configured", with exit code 0, for locations it had just
  started connecting. The wait is spent only where it can help: a location the
  service already knew was not created by the read, so its empty answer is final
  and is judged immediately.
* A directory the service never takes as a location is `not_confirmed`, not "not
  configured": nothing was verified about it either way, so it fails the run and
  the remedy says so instead of advising an MCP entry.
* An HTTP 404 for `/api/mcp` is a **refused location**, not "no servers here".
  Measured: an existing directory the service has never seen answers 200, while a
  path it cannot open answers 404. `OpenCodeAPI.mcp_servers()` no longer swallows
  the 404, and the verdict is `location_refused` with a remedy that names the
  path and the OpenCode build — the old behaviour reported a missing directory as
  "not configured" with exit code 0.
* `--directory` rejects a path that does not exist before asking the service, so
  a stale path is named instead of being materialized as a location.
* A repair no longer waits out the whole settle window (120 s per location) when
  the connection state is empty — no such server, or a dead service. Only
  `pending` is transient, and it is polled for no longer than the client's own
  60 s deadline; a dead service is not contacted at all.
* `--all` now prints why a repair failed, and prints the remedy of **every**
  failing verdict; it used to show a bare "still down", and a remedy only for a
  location whose state could not be read at all, leaving a wedged `pending` or a
  `failed` connect without its own remedy.
* A configured server whose client row carries no state is `unknown_state` with
  the `--fix` remedy, instead of `not_configured` with the advice to add the
  entry that is already there.
* `mcp-health --json` stays parseable when there is nothing to check: the empty
  answer is a JSON object with an `error` field, not prose on stderr.
* Two directories that are the same location are now visited once: the identity
  uses `os.path.realpath`, so an 8.3 short name (`C:\Users\LSZCZE~1\...`) and its
  long form are not repaired (or counted) twice.
* A startup record whose atomic replace collides with a reader is retried for a
  few hundred milliseconds instead of being dropped (Windows refuses the replace
  while another process holds the file open), and a write that still fails leaves
  no `.tmp` file behind.
* A schema reconcile that loses a race with another Perun process's write lock is
  retried three times at startup (the failure used to be swallowed, leaving that
  process on an old schema for its whole life) and is recorded in
  `mcp-startup.json`, so `mcp-health` can name it instead of reporting a healthy
  server with an unmigrated database.
* Nothing is written to disk on the MCP handshake path: the startup record is
  written from the preparation thread, so no file I/O sits in front of the
  `initialize` the client times out.
* The MCP server now answers `initialize` before it touches SQLite. The schema
  reconcile used to run on the import path, where every statement waits up to
  the 30 s busy timeout if another process holds the write lock — right in front
  of a handshake the client abandons after 60 s. It moved to the preparation
  thread (a brand-new home is still created synchronously: no schema, no lock);
  measured start dropped from ~9.5 s to ~3.1 s. FastMCP's startup banner and its
  PyPI version check are also disabled, since both sat in the same budget.
* The generated `handbook.tools` reference refreshes again. FastMCP 2.x replaced
  `list_tools()` with `get_tools()`, so rendering the live registry returned an
  empty body and the context key kept serving a stale copy from before the
  upgrade (missing every tool added since). The handbook reads whichever API the
  installed server offers and takes the argument schema from `parameters` when
  `inputSchema` is absent.
* Context governor no longer mistakes the compaction request for the resulting
  context. Two measurements were wrong: the summariser's own message carries the
  **old** context, and the message page is newest-first, so reversing it read the
  *oldest* turn in the window. Every compaction therefore looked ineffective and
  three in a row disabled the governor. The after-value now comes from the newest
  normal assistant turn that is newer than the summariser message the compact
  call returned (its id is recorded on the event), it waits for a usage snapshot
  that advanced, and unmeasured events or interleaved shadow rows no longer count
  toward the self-disable. Each session is measured once per tick.
* MCP tool modules again expose callable tool names under FastMCP 2.x. The
  decorator returns a `FunctionTool` wrapper, which broke every direct caller
  (tests and the bridge); the module globals now point at the wrapped functions
  while the MCP server keeps its own registry. The proposals tool-name test uses
  `mcp.get_tools()`, the 2.x API.

### Docs

* Documented the two MCP startup failures we hit — a FastMCP 3.x or mixed install
  (`No module named fastmcp.server.extensions`, `PrivateKeyJWTClientAuthenticator`)
  and a handshake frozen by Modern Standby whose failure OpenCode caches per
  project directory — plus the recovery: repair to the pinned `fastmcp>=2.0,<3`,
  then `opencode reload` inside the project. Section 12 now also matches the
  server's tool count (37).

### Fastmcp pin and the memory kernel

* Pin `fastmcp` below 3. The 3.x upgrade broke the MCP server
  (`No module named fastmcp.server.extensions`), taking every `perun_*` tool with
  it; the requirement had no upper bound. A mixed install (3.x leftovers beside
  2.14.7) also failed on `PrivateKeyJWTClientAuthenticator` until the package
  directory was removed and reinstalled.
* Re-release of the memory kernel (call `perun_context`/`perun recall` before
  work, supersede instead of stacking stale facts, CLI fallback when MCP tools are
  missing) so it ships **above** v0.20.1 - v0.19.1 was numerically behind the 0.20
  line and could never reach those installs.

### Global instructions: memory is an input

The Perun kernel (injected into every project) now says what a stale-fact incident
taught us:

* **Memory is an input, not a summary.** Call `perun_context(<intent>)` and
  `perun recall "<topic>"` before starting; when a fact points at a plan or resume
  file, open it instead of re-deriving the state.
* **Supersede, don't stack.** An event that invalidates a stored fact replaces it
  with `perun_memory_supersede`, so the stale version cannot rank first.
* **Missing MCP tools are not a reason to skip memory.** Fall back to the CLI
  (`perun recall|remember|supersede`) and say so.

### Owner workspace: azagor-only push rule

* The git instructions now state that only the `azagor` GitHub account may push
  to `azagor/perun`, `azagor/perun_chat` and `azagor/perun_internal`, and
  document the per-repo credential helper that supplies the azagor token. A
  machine whose active `gh` account belongs to someone else no longer produces
  an avoidable 403 on release.

### PerunChat dashboard: chat with a friend, invite them, and see their chats

* Each friend row now offers **Chat** — opens the bilateral private room (the
  gateway creates it when absent) and joins it in the chat panel — and
  **Add to room…**, which lists the private/group rooms you already belong to
  and invites the friend into the one you pick.
* A **Chats (n)** caret expands the rooms that include that friend, sorted by
  last activity; clicking one opens it. Membership comes from the gateway's
  `member_ids` in one request, and an older gateway is asked once per room with
  the answer cached for the page session (never a request per room on every
  render).
* The chat header and each listed chat show
  `name · participants · last activity`, plus a muted 6-character room id.
  "Last activity" is local truth — this browser's stored transcript for the
  room — because the gateway keeps no durable message timestamps, so an
  untouched room says `no local activity` rather than guessing.
* Both friend actions share a single `openRoomInChat()` helper with the
  private-room card's **Join in chat** button, so a friend chat cannot start a
  second join path or duplicated WebSocket room state.
* The room catalog keeps `joined`, `members`, `type` and `memberIds`. The
  one-pass participant list needs the matching PerunChat gateway change
  (`GET /api/v1/rooms` → `member_ids`); without it the dashboard degrades to
  the cached per-room fallback.
* **Room aliases** (display-only): an inline ✎ on a chat row or the joined
  header stores `perunchat_room_aliases: {room_id: label}` in Perun's own
  settings — never sent to the gateway, and clearing the field removes the
  entry. The alias appears everywhere the room is listed; a destructive
  confirmation still shows `alias (real name/id)`, and room-id keys are
  validated server-side.
* Friends-list layout: the presence dot is its own flex item on the name's
  line, and the action buttons wrap as a group when the card is narrow. A long
  agent id can no longer push the status marker onto a line of its own.
* Hardening from the production audit: saving an alias no longer restarts the
  PerunChat bridge (only a bridge-relevant setting does), stale labels are
  pruned only from a complete room catalog, a transient member-lookup failure
  is not cached for the page, and the gateway's `private:` prefix is accepted
  wherever `priv:` is.

### Picker policy: Perun's own agents stay in their lane

* New `perun/agent_policy.py`, consumed by `/api/agents?surface=` with
  **default-deny**: a request without a surface gets the project rules, so a
  picker that forgets to name its surface fails closed.
  * project (default) - built-ins + agents assigned globally or to that project
  * control - `perun-orchestrator` + built-ins
  * perunchat - the room persona only
  * docs - `perun-docs` only
  * all - unfiltered, explicit
* The dashboard passes its surface explicitly: the orchestrator panel and the
  Settings orchestrator field use `control`, the PerunChat chat persona uses
  `perunchat`. Run, the wizard, coroutines and project surfaces now never offer
  `perun-*`.
* Assignment decisions come from the manifest (`assignments_map()`), so a project
  copy outside the global dirs still counts as assigned.
* Unassigning an agent's **last** placement no longer deletes it: it moves back to
  the library, unassigned, exactly like a fresh install. Only **Remove** deletes.
* Project panel readability: the agent list uses the dark palette (it was black
  text on a dark background), and when every installed agent is global the panel
  says so instead of showing a fully locked list - that is the state where
  nothing is tickable, because the project already inherits everything.

### Installs are unassigned until you place them

* The dashboard's **Install selected** now writes to Perun's **library**
  (`PERUN_HOME/agents/library/`), which OpenCode never reads. A new agent appears
  in no TUI until you assign it - the opt-in model, finally end to end.
  Programmatic `install()` keeps its global default, so nothing else changes.
* Settings -> Installed shows **"N unassigned"** with **Assign all globally**, and
  each row now reads `global`, `project only` or `unassigned`.
* `assign` sources from the library copy, so a library agent can be placed in a
  project or globally; the library file stays as the master and is not counted
  against the registration ceiling (OpenCode never loads it).
* `installed()` returns the `unassigned` list, and `available()` counts a library
  agent as installed.
* Library files are discovered like any other copy (`assignment: "library"`), so
  promote, remove and the assignment fan-out work on them unchanged.

### Assignment refuses Perun's own agents

* `assign` now checks the target through the same protection as every other
  mutation: assigning `perun-orchestrator`, `perun-docs`, `perunchat` or any
  other agent Perun owns is refused with *"a Perun agent; the roster never
  touches it"* instead of reporting a successful assignment.
* Found by the release verification, not by a test: the guard existed for
  remove/promote but not for placement.

### Assign roster agents to projects

* Placement is now explicit. A new `perun/agent_assignments.py` owns it: a copy
  in the global agents directory is a **global** assignment, a copy under
  `<project>/.opencode/agents/` is a **project** assignment, and both are derived
  from where the file lives (the only truth OpenCode reads).
* Settings -> Agent roster -> Installed shows each agent's assignment and a
  **Global** toggle; **Remove** now removes the agent everywhere it is assigned.
* Project config -> **Agents in this project**: tick the agents that project's TUI
  should offer. Globally assigned agents are inherited and shown locked.
* Project copies are **local-only**: the agents directory gets a `.gitignore`
  containing `*`, so `git status` stays clean. Every removal keeps a backup.
* Assigning an agent that is already global to a project is a no-op; unassign and
  remove refuse a copy edited since install.
* `promote` fans the new `mode:` out to every copy.
* API: `POST /api/agent-catalog/{assign,unassign}`, `remove {slug}`. CLI:
  `perun agent-catalog assign|unassign <slug...> --to global|project:<slug>`.
* Install still writes globally in this release; the library/unassigned default
  ships next, with the post-install assign prompt.

### Roster edge cases from the audit

* `promote` / `accept` map an unreadable agent file to a 400 (`could not read …`)
  instead of letting an `OSError` escape as a 500 traceback.
* `_agent_mode` scans 80 frontmatter lines (matching the discovery parser), so a
  long frontmatter still reports its mode and the toggle/badge stay honest.
* Two unit cases pin the edges: an unknown slug is rejected, and an agent with no
  `mode:` reports an empty mode.
